newsitem.title: USA: Senate Democrats to push education programs.
newsitem.headline: Senate Democrats to push education programs.

text.p: Leading Senate Democrats said Thursday education would be their top priority in the next session of Congress and urged Republicans to join them.

"It's time to work together. There is no better place to begin than with our kids, their education and our future. Surely we can all agree on the need to move forward here and that doing so ought to be a bipartisan priority," Sen. Byron Dorgan of North Dakota said at a news conference.

"We share President Clinton's goals of making college more accessible and affordable for all students, modernising school classrooms, helping communities to build new school facilities and repair old ones and helping all children learns to ready by the third grade," Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts added.
Clinton, in a major policy speech on Wednesday, said improving education would be one of his top goals next year, along with balancing the federal budget and passing campaign finance reform laws.
"We are putting education first because the American people believe it is the most important issue facing them and their families," Sen.-elect Jack Reed of Rhode Island said.

Among the specific goals of legislation Democrats will introduce when Congress reconvenes next month are proposals to equip every classroom in the country with computers and to provide tax deductions of up to $10,000 for college tuition for families with incomes below $100,000.
"An additional $2 billion will be invested in schools over the next five years to help close the education technology gap," Kennedy said.
"We intend to introduce these proposals on Day One of the next Congress and to work vigorously to enact them as soon as possible," he said.
Separately, Democratic Representative Frank Pallone of New Jersey said he would introduce legislation to provide health insurance for the 10 million uninsured American children.

"Too many kids today are falling through the cracks when it comes to health insurance coverage. Many working families do not receive coverage through work and, because they are above the poverty line, do not qualify for Medicaid," Pallone said in a statement.
